q: A 28-year-old patient presents with a non-tender, indurated ulcer on the shaft of the penis and generalized lymphadenopathy. The DIS should classify this patient as having:
Which of the following clinical signs is NOT typically associated with secondary syphilis?

According to the staging framework, a patient has no symptoms, a reactive treponemal test, and a reactive nontreponemal test. The patient had a documented negative RPR 8 months ago. How should the case be staged?

A patient has a reactive treponemal test and current RPR of 1:2. Medical history shows a documented RPR of 1:16 six months ago. Does this meet supportive laboratory criteria for a new early infection?

options.text: No; this is a fourfold decrease, not a fourfold increase
No; a treponemal test alone is required

q: Which laboratory pattern generally provides presumptive serologic evidence of syphilis infection for stages requiring both serologic test types?

options.text: A reactive treponemal test and a reactive nontreponemal test

q: For a patient diagnosed with secondary syphilis, what is the standard sexual contact interview period used for partner services in many DIS protocols?
A patient is diagnosed with primary syphilis. A sexual partner from 75 days ago is identified. According to standard partner management protocols, this partner should:

options.text: Be presumptively treated according to local protocol

q: A DIS is interviewing a patient with early non-primary non-secondary syphilis. The patient reports having a new painless chancre four months ago that went away on its own. When defining the critical period and staging rationale, this is best documented as:
According to the reporting change discussed in training, congenital syphilis cases are classified/reported based on:

options.text: The state where the mother first tested positive
The state where prenatal care began

q: An infant has a reactive RPR of 1:4, and the mother had untreated syphilis at delivery. The infant is asymptomatic. This case is:

options.text: Not a case; positive IgM is required
Not a case if the infant has no symptoms

q: Scenario: A patient presents with a genital chancre and a diffuse copper-colored rash involving the trunk, palms, and soles. Current RPR is reactive and treponemal test is reactive. What stage should be selected?

options.text: Primary Syphilis, because the chancre is present
Early Non-Primary Non-Secondary, because more than one sign is present

q: Scenario: A patient is asymptomatic. Current treponemal test is reactive and current RPR is reactive. A prior RPR from 13 months ago was negative. There are no documented symptoms, no partner linkage, and no other evidence that acquisition occurred within the previous 12 months. What is the correct stage?

Scenario: A patient has no current signs. Current RPR and treponemal test are reactive. During the interview, the patient clearly describes a painless genital ulcer 7 months ago that lasted 2 weeks and resolved without treatment. Write the likely stage AND the specific type of acquisition evidence being used.

Scenario: Patient has a classic palmar/plantar rash and mucous patches. Current RPR is 1:64. No treponemal test has been ordered yet. There is no concurrent nonreactive treponemal result. What is the best classification path?

options.text: Probable Secondary Syphilis, Path B: clinical criteria plus RPR >=1:32 with treponemal absent/pending
Confirmed Secondary Syphilis, because RPR is >=1:32
Early Non-Primary Non-Secondary, because treponemal testing is missing
Not a case until a treponemal result is reactive

q: Scenario: A patient has no current primary or secondary symptoms. Current RPR and treponemal test are reactive. The patient reports sexual exposure 4 months ago to a partner independently documented as having secondary syphilis. Write the stage AND the acquisition criterion used.

Scenario: An asymptomatic patient has current reactive RPR and reactive treponemal test. There is no documented history of syphilis and no evidence of acquisition within the previous 12 months. Which classification path best applies?

options.text: Early Non-Primary Non-Secondary, because the serology is reactive
Syphilis, Unknown Duration - Probable Path A: no documented history plus presumptive serology and no <=12-month acquisition evidence

q: Scenario: A patient has no current primary or secondary signs. RPR and treponemal test are reactive. There is no evidence of acquisition within the previous 12 months. The patient reports new vision changes and an ophthalmologist documents posterior uveitis on examination. No direct-detection laboratory testing was performed on the affected fluid. Write the base stage, the appropriate sub-classification, AND whether that sub-classification should be recorded as likely or verified (probable or confirmed).

Scenario: Patient has reactive RPR and reactive treponemal test, neurologic signs consistent with meningovascular syphilis, and CSF RPR is reactive in a specimen without visible blood contamination. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: CSF RPR can support Verified Neurologic Syphilis under the current framework
CSF RPR is ignored; only CSF VDRL can be used
Neurologic manifestations are additive and do not replace the base syphilis stage
This automatically makes the base stage Primary Syphilis

q: Scenario: Patient has a diffuse rash consistent with secondary syphilis and current RPR of 1:64. A treponemal test returns nonreactive. Explain whether Secondary Probable Path B is still available AND why.

Scenario: A case was initially staged as Syphilis, Unknown Duration because there was no evidence of acquisition within the previous 12 months. During a later DIS interview, the patient gives a specific, credible history of a painless genital ulcer 6 months ago. There are no current primary or secondary signs. What should the DIS do?

options.text: Keep Unknown Duration because staging cannot be changed after initial entry
Re-stage as Early Non-Primary Non-Secondary using prior primary signs within 12 months as acquisition evidence
Re-stage as Primary Syphilis because the patient once had a chancre
